# Amazon S3: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q003 -->
### Question 1

A company runs a photo-sharing mobile app. The app's backend runs on Amazon EC2 instances that use an IAM role. Users must upload photos from the app directly to a private Amazon S3 bucket, without sending the photos through the backend. The users do not have AWS credentials. Each upload must be allowed for a short, temporary period. Which solution will allow the uploads in the MOST secure way?

- Create an IAM user that can call s3:PutObject on the bucket, and store the user's access key in the app to sign each upload.
- Add a bucket policy that allows s3:PutObject for every principal on an uploads prefix, and turn off Block Public Access for the bucket.
- Have the backend use its IAM role to presign a URL for one object key with a short expiry, and return the URL to the app.
- Let a developer presign upload URLs with the longest expiry from the developer's IAM user, and ship the URLs inside the app.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Have the backend use its IAM role to presign a URL for one object key with a short expiry, and return the URL to the app.

**Deciding phrases.** "directly to a private Amazon S3 bucket", "do not have AWS credentials", "short, temporary period", "MOST secure"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST secure way to allow the uploads.
2. I mark the constraints: the bucket stays private, the photos skip the backend, the users have no AWS credentials, and each upload is allowed for a short time.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a presigned URL, because it lets someone upload one object without AWS credentials of their own.
4. I remove the public bucket policy, because a wildcard principal means anyone and the bucket must stay private. I remove the IAM user, because its access key is a long-term credential inside every copy of the app.
5. Between the two presigned URL options the difference is who signs and for how long; the stem says a short, temporary period, so the backend signs one URL for each upload with its role and a short expiry.
6. Check: the presigned URL from the backend meets every constraint and keeps the bucket private. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The backend signs each URL with its role, so no user needs AWS credentials. A presigned URL gives [time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials) without a change to the bucket policy, and it is [limited by the permissions of the user](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-creator-needs-permission) or role that signed it. A short expiry for one object key keeps each link narrow.

**Why not.**

- "Create an IAM user that can call s3:PutObject ...": Every copy of the app would hold a long-term key, and AWS advises that you [use an IAM role to manage temporary credentials](../facts/s3.md#s3-best-practice-iam-roles-not-stored-credentials) instead.
- "Add a bucket policy that allows s3:PutObject for ...": The uploads work, but a wildcard principal [which effectively means "anyone"](../facts/s3.md#s3-best-practice-wildcard-principal-means-anyone) lets anyone write, so the bucket is no longer private.
- "Let a developer presign upload URLs with the ...": It works, but a presigned URL can be used [multiple times, up to the expiration date](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-reusable-until-expiry), so a shipped URL lets anyone upload for days.

**Twin.** If the stem said "users download a private photo" instead: the backend presigns a GET URL, because a presigned URL gives [time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials) for reads too.

**Takeaway.** Users without AWS credentials upload to a private bucket through a short-lived presigned URL from the backend.

**Review.** [A presigned URL lends the permission of its signer until the URL expires](2-deep.md#a-presigned-url-lends-the-permission-of-its-signer-until-the-url-expires-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company stores customer contracts in an Amazon S3 bucket and relies on the durability of Amazon S3 to protect them. Last month, an employee deleted several contracts by mistake, and another employee overwrote a contract with the wrong file. The company could not recover any of them. The company must be able to recover from accidental deletes and overwrites in the future. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Run a nightly script that copies every object in the bucket to a second bucket in another AWS Region for recovery.
- Make no change to the bucket, because S3 durability already keeps several copies of every object across Availability Zones.
- Turn on S3 Versioning for the bucket, and add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after a set number of days.
- Add a bucket policy that denies the s3:DeleteObject action to every principal in the account, except the security team.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on S3 Versioning for the bucket, and add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after a set number of days.

**Deciding phrases.** "relies on the durability", "accidental deletes and overwrites", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead that recovers from deletes and overwrites.
2. I mark the constraints: the company relies on durability, both deletes and overwrites happened, and recovery must work from now on.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict no change, because S3 durability already keeps several copies of every object.
4. I remove the bucket policy, because an overwrite is a PUT request and the policy stops deletes only. I remove the nightly script, because it adds work and loses the changes of each day.
5. Between making no change and turning on versioning, the difference is what durability protects. My first idea breaks because durability does not protect against accidental or malicious deletes, and a deleted object cannot be recovered by AWS, so I choose versioning, which keeps every version of every object.
6. Check: versioning meets every constraint, and the lifecycle rule stops old versions from growing without limit. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Durability protects against hardware loss, but it [does not protect against accidental or malicious deletes](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-durability-not-delete-protection). S3 Versioning keeps [every version of every object](../facts/s3.md#s3-data-protection-mechanisms), so you can [recover from both unintended user actions](../facts/s3.md#s3-data-protection-mechanisms) and application failures. A delete adds a delete marker, an overwrite keeps the older version, and a lifecycle rule limits the cost of old versions.

**Why not.**

- "Run a nightly script that copies every object ...": It helps after a delete, but a script is more work to run, and changes made during the day are lost before the next copy.
- "Make no change to the bucket, because S3 ...": Durability [does not protect against accidental or malicious deletes](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-durability-not-delete-protection), and a deleted object [cannot be recovered by AWS](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-delete-is-immediate).
- "Add a bucket policy that denies the s3:DeleteObject ...": The policy stops deletes, but an overwrite is a PUT request, so a wrong file still replaces a contract and leaves no older copy.

**Twin.** If the stem said "no user, including administrators, can delete a contract for 7 years" instead: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, because a locked version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode).

**Takeaway.** Durability is not a backup; turn on versioning to recover from deletes and overwrites.

**Review.** [Versioning turns a delete into a delete marker and keeps every version](2-deep.md#versioning-turns-a-delete-into-a-delete-marker-and-keeps-every-version-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company turned on S3 Cross-Region Replication from a bucket in one AWS Region to a bucket in a second Region. Versioning is turned on for both buckets. The source bucket already held 2 years of objects when the replication rule was created. New objects now appear in the destination bucket, but the older objects do not. The company must replicate the older objects too. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Suspend versioning on the destination bucket and turn it on again, so that the replication rule starts again for all objects.
- Turn on S3 Replication Time Control for the replication rule, so that S3 replicates the older objects to the destination within a set time.
- Write a script that lists every object in the source bucket and copies each object to the destination bucket with the AWS CLI.
- Create an S3 Batch Replication job for the replication rule, so that S3 replicates the objects that existed before the rule was created.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an S3 Batch Replication job for the replication rule, so that S3 replicates the objects that existed before the rule was created.

**Deciding phrases.** "already held 2 years of objects", "New objects now appear in the destination bucket", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The rule works for new objects, so versioning and permissions are in place. Live replication [replicates newly uploaded objects as they are written](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects). The objects that existed before the rule need S3 Batch Replication, which [allows you to replicate existing objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects) through S3 Batch Operations jobs.

**Why not.**

- "Suspend versioning on the destination bucket and turn ...": Versioning is already on, and while it is off [on the destination bucket, replication fails](../facts/s3.md#s3-replication-requires-versioning-both-buckets); a restart copies no older objects.
- "Turn on S3 Replication Time Control for the ...": RTC sets a time target for live replication, which [replicates newly uploaded objects as they are written](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects); it does not reach older objects.
- "Write a script that lists every object in ...": It works, but a script is code to write, run and check, while Batch Replication [allows you to replicate existing objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-batch-replication-for-existing-objects) as a managed job.

**Twin.** If the stem said "new objects must replicate within a predictable time" instead: turn on S3 Replication Time Control, which is [enabled as an option for each replication rule](../facts/s3.md#s3-replication-time-control-15-minutes).

**Takeaway.** Replication copies new objects; S3 Batch Replication copies the objects that were in the bucket before the rule.

**Review.** [Replication copies new objects asynchronously and needs versioning on both buckets](2-deep.md#replication-copies-new-objects-asynchronously-and-needs-versioning-on-both-buckets-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company has 200 Amazon S3 buckets in one AWS account. Developers sometimes add bucket policies that allow public reads, and the security team finds them weeks later. Only the security team can change account-level settings. The company must ensure that no bucket in the account can be made public by a bucket policy, now or in the future. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an AWS Config rule that checks each bucket policy for public access, and report the noncompliant buckets to the security team.
- Turn on IAM Access Analyzer for S3, and send an alert to the security team when a bucket policy allows public access.
- Turn on all four S3 Block Public Access settings at the account level, so that the settings apply to every bucket in the account.
- Turn on all four S3 Block Public Access settings on each bucket, and turn them on for each new bucket after it is created.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on all four S3 Block Public Access settings at the account level, so that the settings apply to every bucket in the account.

**Deciding phrases.** "must ensure that no bucket in the account can be made public", "now or in the future", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Block Public Access stops a public policy instead of reporting it. At the account level, the setting [applies to all buckets and access points](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-account-level-recommended) that the account owns, and Block Public Access [settings override these policies and permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-overrides-policies). The developers have no access to account settings, so the protection holds for buckets created later.

**Why not.**

- "Create an AWS Config rule that checks each ...": A Config rule evaluates a bucket after the change and does not block the bucket policy, so a bucket can still become public.
- "Turn on IAM Access Analyzer for S3, and ...": [IAM Access Analyzer for S3](../facts/s3.md#s3-access-analyzer-public-or-other-accounts) reports a public bucket after the policy exists; an alert does not stop the policy.
- "Turn on all four S3 Block Public Access ...": It works for today's buckets, but every new bucket adds a step, while an account setting [applies to all buckets and access points](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-account-level-recommended) at once.

**Twin.** If the stem said "every account in an organization" instead: use [organization-level enforcement through AWS Organizations](../facts/s3.md#s3-block-public-access-centralized-controls) for Block Public Access.

**Takeaway.** To prevent public buckets in an account, turn on Block Public Access at the account level; alerts detect but do not prevent.

**Review.** [Block Public Access overrides any policy or ACL that would make data public](2-deep.md#block-public-access-overrides-any-policy-or-acl-that-would-make-data-public-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A financial services company stores trade records as objects in a new Amazon S3 bucket. An application uploads thousands of records each day. The company must retain each record in an immutable form for 7 years. No user, including the root user, can be allowed to delete or overwrite a record before the end of its retention period. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, and change the application so that every upload request sets compliance mode and a retain-until date 7 years ahead.
- Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, change the application so that every upload sets governance mode and a 7-year retain-until date, and let only the security team bypass it.
- Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in compliance mode, and set a default retention period of 7 years that applies to every new object version.
- Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in governance mode, set a default retention period of 7 years, and allow only the security team to bypass governance retention.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in compliance mode, and set a default retention period of 7 years that applies to every new object version.

**Deciding phrases.** "including the root user", "retain each record in an immutable form", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The deciding phrase is the root user. In compliance mode a locked version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), and [its retention period can't be shortened](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode). A bucket default retention sets [how long to protect every object version](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-bucket-default-retention) that arrives later, so the application needs no change.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, ...": It works, but changing the application to set [a unique retention period for individual objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-retention-per-object-or-bucket-default) is more work than a bucket default.
- "Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, ...": Governance mode stops users [unless they have special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode), so the security team can still delete, and the application change adds work.
- "Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket ...": In governance mode, users cannot delete a locked version [unless they have special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode), so the security team could still delete records.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the security team must be able to remove the protection when a legal request requires it" instead: governance mode with the bypass permission, because it protects versions [unless they have special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode).

**Takeaway.** Not even the root user can delete: use Object Lock compliance mode with a bucket default retention.

**Review.** [Object Lock compliance mode stops every user from deleting a version until its date](2-deep.md#object-lock-compliance-mode-stops-every-user-from-deleting-a-version-until-its-date-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company stores product images in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each image is larger than 1 MB. The images are infrequently accessed: a user opens each image about once a month. When a user opens an image, the image must load in milliseconds. The images are thumbnails that the company can generate again from the original files at any time. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?

- Store the images in S3 Standard-IA, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.
- Store the images in S3 One Zone-IA, which stores data in a single Availability Zone and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.
- Store the images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which has the lowest storage price of all the S3 storage classes.
- Store the images in S3 Standard, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges no retrieval fee.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Store the images in S3 One Zone-IA, which stores data in a single Availability Zone and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.

**Deciding phrases.** "can generate again from the original files", "must load in milliseconds", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The thumbnails can be generated again, so the loss of one Availability Zone is acceptable. S3 One Zone-IA fits data when you can [re-create the data if the Availability Zone fails](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use), keeps objects [available for millisecond access](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-classes-millisecond-access-retrieval-fee), and costs less than S3 Standard-IA. Each image is larger than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size), so the minimum billable size does not change the choice.

**Why not.**

- "Store the images in S3 Standard-IA, which stores ...": It works, but the thumbnails can be generated again, and S3 One Zone-IA costs [20% less than S3 Standard-IA](../facts/s3.md#s3-one-zone-ia-single-az-20-percent-cheaper).
- "Store the images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, ...": Before a read, you [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), so no image loads in milliseconds.
- "Store the images in S3 Standard, which stores ...": It works, but S3 Standard is for data read [more than once a month](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-standard-profile), so it costs more to store these images.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The images are the only copy, and they must remain available if an Availability Zone is lost" instead: S3 Standard-IA, because it is for the [primary or only copy of data](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use).

**Takeaway.** For infrequently read data, S3 One Zone-IA fits copies you can re-create, and S3 Standard-IA fits the primary copy.

**Review.** [Infrequent access classes add retrieval fees and a minimum storage duration](2-deep.md#infrequent-access-classes-add-retrieval-fees-and-a-minimum-storage-duration-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company stores product images in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each image is larger than 1 MB. The images are infrequently accessed: a user opens each image about once a month. When a user opens an image, the image must load in milliseconds. The images are the only copy, and they must remain available if an Availability Zone is lost. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective choice that meets these requirements?

- Store the images in S3 Standard-IA, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.
- Store the images in S3 One Zone-IA, which stores data in a single Availability Zone and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.
- Store the images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which has the lowest storage price of all the S3 storage classes.
- Store the images in S3 Standard, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges no retrieval fee.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Store the images in S3 Standard-IA, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones and charges a per-GB retrieval fee.

**Deciding phrases.** "the only copy", "must remain available if an Availability Zone is lost", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The stem makes the loss of an Availability Zone unacceptable. AWS recommends S3 Standard-IA for the [primary or only copy of data](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-primary-copy), and its objects stay [available for millisecond access](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-classes-millisecond-access-retrieval-fee). Each image is larger than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size), so the minimum billable size does not change the choice.

**Why not.**

- "Store the images in S3 One Zone-IA, which ...": S3 One Zone-IA is [not resilient to the physical loss](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use) of its zone, so the only copy can disappear with that zone.
- "Store the images in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, ...": Before a read, you [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), so no image loads in milliseconds.
- "Store the images in S3 Standard, which stores ...": It works, but S3 Standard is for data read [more than once a month](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-standard-profile), so it costs more to store these images.

**Twin.** If the stem said "thumbnails that the company can generate again from the original files at any time" instead: S3 One Zone-IA, because you can [re-create the data if the Availability Zone fails](../facts/s3.md#s3-standard-ia-vs-one-zone-ia-use).

**Takeaway.** The primary copy of infrequently read data goes to S3 Standard-IA, not to S3 One Zone-IA.

**Review.** [Infrequent access classes add retrieval fees and a minimum storage duration](2-deep.md#infrequent-access-classes-add-retrieval-fees-and-a-minimum-storage-duration-5-min)

</details>

### Question 8

A company runs a media library in an Amazon S3 bucket. The bucket is the only copy of the files, and each file is larger than 10 MB. Some files are read many times each day for months. Other files are never read after their first week. Nobody can predict which files will stay popular, so the access pattern of each file is unpredictable. Which storage approach is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Store the files in S3 Standard, and add a lifecycle rule that moves every file to S3 Standard-IA 30 days after upload.
- Store the files in S3 One Zone-IA, because it costs less than S3 Standard-IA and keeps the same eleven nines of durability.
- Store the files in S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so that S3 moves each file between access tiers based on how often the file is read.
- Store the files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and serve each file to users with a normal GET request when they ask for it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Store the files in S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so that S3 moves each file between access tiers based on how often the file is read.

**Deciding phrases.** "the access pattern of each file is unpredictable", "the only copy of the files", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** S3 Intelligent-Tiering [automatically stores objects in three access tiers](../facts/s3.md#s3-intelligent-tiering-automatic-tiers) and watches how often each object is read. A file that is read again is [automatically moved back to the Frequent Access tier](../facts/s3.md#s3-int-tiering-move-back), so a popular file returns to the fast tier. Objects smaller than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-int-tiering-small-objects) are not tiered, but every file here is larger.

**Why not.**

- "Store the files in S3 Standard, and add ...": Popular files are still read after day 30, and S3 Standard-IA adds a [per-GB retrieval charge](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-standard-ia-retrieval-charge) to each of those reads.
- "Store the files in S3 One Zone-IA, because ...": The bucket is the only copy, and S3 One Zone-IA is [not resilient to the physical loss](../facts/s3.md#s3-one-zone-ia-az-loss) of its Availability Zone.
- "Store the files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, ...": A normal GET does not read this class: first you [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), which takes hours.

**Twin.** If the stem said "every file is read about once a month" instead: S3 Standard-IA, because the pattern is known and the class suits data read [once a month](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-standard-ia-profile).

**Takeaway.** An unknown or changing access pattern points to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which charges no retrieval fee.

**Review.** [Intelligent-Tiering moves an unread object to cheaper tiers with no retrieval fee](2-deep.md#intelligent-tiering-moves-an-unread-object-to-cheaper-tiers-with-no-retrieval-fee-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A financial services company stores trade records as objects in a new Amazon S3 bucket. An application uploads thousands of records each day. The company must retain each record in an immutable form for 7 years. Most users must not be able to delete or overwrite a record, but the security team must be able to remove the protection when a legal request requires it. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, and change the application so that every upload request sets compliance mode and a retain-until date 7 years ahead.
- Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, change the application so that every upload sets governance mode and a 7-year retain-until date, and let only the security team bypass it.
- Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in compliance mode, and set a default retention period of 7 years that applies to every new object version.
- Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in governance mode, set a default retention period of 7 years, and allow only the security team to bypass governance retention.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in governance mode, set a default retention period of 7 years, and allow only the security team to bypass governance retention.

**Deciding phrases.** "the security team must be able to remove the protection", "retain each record in an immutable form", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** AWS says to use governance mode when [some users with special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-mode-choice) can alter the retention or delete objects. A user who holds [s3:BypassGovernanceRetention](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode) and sends the [x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode) header can remove the protection. The bucket default sets [how long to protect every object version](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-bucket-default-retention), so the application needs no change.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, ...": Every upload sets compliance mode, and a version in that mode [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), so the security team is locked out as well.
- "Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, ...": It works, but changing the application to set [a unique retention period for individual objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-retention-per-object-or-bucket-default) is more work than a bucket default.
- "Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket ...": A version in compliance mode [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), so the security team cannot remove the protection for a legal request.

**Twin.** If the stem said "No user, including the root user, can be allowed to delete or overwrite a record" instead: compliance mode, because a version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode).

**Takeaway.** When a privileged team needs to remove the lock, use governance mode and give that team the bypass permission.

**Review.** [Object Lock compliance mode stops every user from deleting a version until its date](2-deep.md#object-lock-compliance-mode-stops-every-user-from-deleting-a-version-until-its-date-4-min)

</details>

### Question 10

A company stores signed contracts as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company manages its own keys in a hardware security module in its data center. Company policy says that the encryption keys must never be stored in AWS. Each object must be encrypted before it leaves the data center, so that AWS never sees unencrypted data in transit or at rest. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key in AWS KMS, and let the company's security team control the key policy and the key rotation.
- Turn on SSE-C for the bucket, and send the company's key over HTTPS with every upload request and every download request.
- Encrypt each object in the data center with the company's key before upload, and decrypt it in the data center after download.
- Encrypt each object in the data center before upload, and also turn on SSE-C and send the company's key with every request.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Encrypt each object in the data center with the company's key before upload, and decrypt it in the data center after download.

**Deciding phrases.** "keys must never be stored in AWS", "encrypted before it leaves the data center", "LEAST development effort"

**Why.** The stem keeps unencrypted data away from AWS, so the encryption happens before upload. With client-side encryption, [you manage the encryption process, the encryption keys](../facts/s3.md#s3-client-side-encryption-you-manage-keys) and the tools, and S3 [does not play a role in encrypting](../facts/s3.md#s3-client-side-encryption-not-exposed-to-aws) the objects. S3 stores ciphertext, and the key stays in the hardware security module.

**Why not.**

- "Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key in ...": Customer managed does not mean kept by the company: the KMS key lives in AWS KMS, [in the same Region as the bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-kms-key-same-region-as-bucket).
- "Turn on SSE-C for the bucket, and send ...": With SSE-C, S3 receives the plaintext and encrypts it on arrival, so AWS sees unencrypted data, even though [S3 never stores the encryption key](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required).
- "Encrypt each object in the data center before ...": It works, because client-side encryption keeps plaintext away from AWS, but the extra SSE-C layer adds key handling on every request that the stem does not need.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Amazon S3 must encrypt each object at rest and decrypt it" instead: SSE-C, because S3 does the work and [S3 never stores the encryption key](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required).

**Takeaway.** Plaintext stays inside the company: encrypt client-side before upload.

**Review.** [Every new object is encrypted with SSE-S3 unless you choose another key](2-deep.md#every-new-object-is-encrypted-with-sse-s3-unless-you-choose-another-key-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

## Extended

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q019 -->
### Question 11

A company runs a video editing service. Users around the world upload project files of 2 GB to 20 GB to one Amazon S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region. Users who are far from the Region report slow uploads that do not use their full bandwidth. The company wants faster uploads to the same bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a bucket in a Region near each group of users, and replicate each bucket to the us-east-1 bucket with Cross-Region Replication.
- Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, and change the upload clients to use the accelerate endpoint of the bucket.
- Order an AWS Direct Connect connection from each user location to the us-east-1 Region, and send the uploads over those connections.
- Change the upload clients to send each file in one PUT request instead of many parts, to cut the number of round trips.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, and change the upload clients to use the accelerate endpoint of the bucket.

**Deciding phrases.** "Users around the world", "do not use their full bandwidth", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Transfer Acceleration is made for customers who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use) from all over the world. Uploads enter the [globally distributed edge locations in Amazon CloudFront](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works) and reach the bucket [over an optimized network path](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works). It is one bucket setting and a new endpoint in the clients.

**Why not.**

- "Create a bucket in a Region near each ...": It works, but every new bucket and replication rule is more to manage, while Transfer Acceleration is one setting on the existing bucket.
- "Order an AWS Direct Connect connection from each ...": Direct Connect suits private networking, and Transfer Acceleration suits [distributed client locations over the public internet](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-ta-vs-direct-connect), such as these users.
- "Change the upload clients to send each file ...": One PUT request uploads an object of [5 GB](../facts/s3.md#s3-single-put-max) at most, so a 20 GB file cannot go in one request.

**Twin.** If the stem said "files smaller than 1 GB" instead: consider CloudFront PUT/POST, which AWS suggests for objects [smaller than 1 GB](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-vs-cloudfront-small-objects).

**Takeaway.** Slow long-distance uploads to one bucket point to S3 Transfer Acceleration.

**Review.** [A single PUT stops at 5 GB so large uploads use multipart upload](2-deep.md#a-single-put-stops-at-5-gb-so-large-uploads-use-multipart-upload-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q012 -->
### Question 12

A company stores daily sales exports in an Amazon S3 bucket in account A. ACLs are disabled on the bucket, and the objects are encrypted with SSE-S3. A reporting application runs as an AWS Lambda function in account B and uses an execution role. The application must read the exports, and the security team requires least privilege. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST securely? (Select TWO.)

- Add the canonical user ID of account B to the ACL of each export object with read permission, and leave the bucket policy unchanged.
- Add a statement to the bucket policy in account A that allows s3:GetObject on the export objects for the ARN of the execution role.
- Add a statement to the bucket policy in account A that allows s3:GetObject for the wildcard principal when the user agent names account B.
- Add a statement to the identity-based policy of the execution role in account B that allows s3:GetObject on the export objects.
- Create an IAM user in account A with read access to the bucket, and store the access key of the user in an environment variable of the function.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Add a statement to the bucket policy in account A that allows s3:GetObject on the export objects for the ARN of the execution role.
- Add a statement to the identity-based policy of the execution role in account B that allows s3:GetObject on the export objects.

**Deciding phrases.** "bucket in account A", "Lambda function in account B", "least privilege", "MOST securely"

**Why.** The role is in account B and the bucket is in account A. A principal needs [permission from both the parent AWS account](../facts/s3.md#s3-authorization-both-accounts-must-allow) and the account that owns the bucket. So account A names the role in its bucket policy, and account B allows the action in the role's policy.

- The bucket owner has to agree: S3 needs [permission from both the parent AWS account](../facts/s3.md#s3-authorization-both-accounts-must-allow) and account A, and this statement names one role.
- The role's own account has to allow the action as well, because S3 needs [permission from both the parent AWS account](../facts/s3.md#s3-authorization-both-accounts-must-allow) and the bucket owner.

**Why not.**

- "Add the canonical user ID of account B ...": ACLs are disabled, so [you must use policies to grant access](../facts/s3.md#s3-acl-writes-fail-when-bucket-owner-enforced), and a request that sets an ACL fails.
- "Add a statement to the bucket policy in ...": A wildcard principal with Allow reaches all users, [including anonymous users (public access)](../facts/iam.md#iam-principal-wildcard-is-public), and any caller can send that user agent.
- "Create an IAM user in account A with ...": It works, but stored access keys [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire), which is less secure than the execution role.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the objects are encrypted with SSE-KMS and the AWS managed key" instead: re-encrypt them, because cross-account readers need you to [use a customer managed key](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-kms-cross-account-needs-customer-managed-key).

**Takeaway.** Cross-account S3 reads need an allow in the bucket policy and in the caller's identity-based policy.

**Review.** [S3 allows a request only when a policy allows it and nothing denies it](2-deep.md#s3-allows-a-request-only-when-a-policy-allows-it-and-nothing-denies-it-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q020 -->
### Question 13

A company receives order files from partners in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each new file must start a processing job. The processing team runs workers that read from an existing Amazon SQS FIFO queue, and the team will not change the workers. The company wants to decouple the upload side from the processing side and does not need S3 to keep events in order. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Configure an S3 event notification for object-created events that sends each event directly to the SQS FIFO queue as its destination.
- Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function, and write code in the function that sends each event to the SQS FIFO queue.
- Turn on Amazon EventBridge delivery for the bucket, and create an EventBridge rule that matches object-created events and targets the SQS FIFO queue.
- Write an AWS Lambda function that lists the bucket every minute, finds the new files, and sends a message to the SQS FIFO queue for each one.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on Amazon EventBridge delivery for the bucket, and create an EventBridge rule that matches object-created events and targets the SQS FIFO queue.

**Deciding phrases.** "an existing Amazon SQS FIFO queue", "will not change the workers", "LEAST development effort"

**Why.** S3 event notifications cannot target the queue, because [FIFO (First-In-First-Out) queues aren't supported](../facts/s3.md#s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations). For that case AWS says [you can use Amazon EventBridge](../facts/s3.md#s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations). EventBridge receives every event of the bucket, and a rule with the FIFO queue as its target forwards the object-created events. The setup is configuration, with no function to write.

**Why not.**

- "Configure an S3 event notification for object-created events ...": An SQS FIFO queue is not a valid notification destination: [FIFO (First-In-First-Out) queues aren't supported](../facts/s3.md#s3-event-notifications-no-fifo-destinations).
- "Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an ...": It works, but the Lambda function is code to write and maintain, and an EventBridge rule reaches the FIFO queue without code.
- "Write an AWS Lambda function that lists the ...": It works, but polling needs custom code and repeated list requests, and it reacts later than an event rule that fires for each new object.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an existing Amazon SQS standard queue" instead: an S3 event notification sent directly to the queue, because events can go to [Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-events-destinations).

**Takeaway.** S3 events for an SQS FIFO queue go through Amazon EventBridge and a rule.

**Review.** [A single PUT stops at 5 GB so large uploads use multipart upload](2-deep.md#a-single-put-stops-at-5-gb-so-large-uploads-use-multipart-upload-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q015 -->
### Question 14

A research institute stores a large genomics dataset in an Amazon S3 bucket. Partner organizations download parts of the dataset into their own AWS accounts in several AWS Regions. The institute's bill for requests and data transfer grows every month because of these downloads. The institute wants to avoid paying for the partners' requests and downloads, and the partners agree to pay for them. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Move the dataset to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so that the cost of the partners' downloads goes down as access patterns change.
- Generate presigned URLs with the institute's IAM role for the objects that each partner needs, and send the URLs to the partners.
- Replicate the dataset with S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in each partner's account in the partner's Region.
- Turn on Requester Pays for the bucket, and allow the partner accounts to read the dataset in the bucket policy.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on Requester Pays for the bucket, and allow the partner accounts to read the dataset in the bucket policy.

**Deciding phrases.** "wants to avoid paying for the partners' requests and downloads", "their own AWS accounts", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The bucket owner pays for requests and downloads unless the bucket is [Requester Pays](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-cross-account-access-billing). With Requester Pays, [the requester instead of the bucket owner pays](../facts/s3.md#s3-requester-pays-who-pays) for the request and the download, and the institute keeps paying for storage. Because [anonymous access to that bucket is not allowed](../facts/s3.md#s3-requester-pays-no-anonymous), the partners sign requests with their AWS accounts.

**Why not.**

- "Move the dataset to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so that ...": A storage class changes the storage price, not the payer; normal pricing applies unless the bucket is [Requester Pays](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-cross-account-access-billing).
- "Generate presigned URLs with the institute's IAM role ...": The URLs work, but each one uses the credentials of the [principal who generated the URL](../facts/s3.md#s3-presigned-url-time-limited-creator-credentials), so the institute stays the payer.
- "Replicate the dataset with S3 Cross-Region Replication to ...": Each partner gets a copy, but in cross-account replication [the source account pays for all data transfer](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-replication-cross-account-who-pays), so the institute pays for every copy.

**Twin.** If the stem said "anyone on the internet downloads the dataset" instead: Requester Pays does not fit, because [anonymous access to that bucket is not allowed](../facts/s3.md#s3-requester-pays-no-anonymous).

**Takeaway.** To share a bucket and let other AWS accounts pay for their downloads, turn on Requester Pays.

**Review.** [Access points and Requester Pays control who reaches shared data and who pays](2-deep.md#access-points-and-requester-pays-control-who-reaches-shared-data-and-who-pays-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q021 -->
### Question 15

A company runs a batch job once a day that writes about 1 million JSON result files to an Amazon S3 bucket in S3 Standard. Each file is about 20 KB. An analytics job reads all the results of one day together. After the first week, the results are infrequently accessed, about once a month, and each read must return data in milliseconds. The company wants to lower the storage cost of results that are older than 30 days. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 KB result file to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days, which has the lowest storage price.
- Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 KB result file to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, with an object size filter that includes the small files.
- Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 KB result file to S3 Intelligent-Tiering after 30 days, so that unread files move to cheaper tiers.
- Combine each day's results into one large object before upload, and add a lifecycle rule that moves these objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Combine each day's results into one large object before upload, and add a lifecycle rule that moves these objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days.

**Deciding phrases.** "Each file is about 20 KB", "reads all the results of one day together", "must return data in milliseconds", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA bill each object as at least [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size), so they suit larger objects. A 20 KB file is billed for more than six times its size there, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering keeps it in the Frequent Access tier. The analytics job reads one day at a time, so one object per day keeps the reads simple and lets the lifecycle rule lower the storage cost.

**Why not.**

- "Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 ...": Before a read, you [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), so no read returns data in milliseconds.
- "Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 ...": The files move, but S3 Standard-IA bills each object as at least [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size), more than six times the size of each file.
- "Add a lifecycle rule that moves each 20 ...": S3 Intelligent-Tiering keeps an object smaller than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-int-tiering-small-objects) in the Frequent Access tier, so these files never reach a cheaper tier.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each file is about 5 MB" instead: a lifecycle rule can move each file to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, because the [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-ia-min-billable-size) minimum adds no cost.

**Takeaway.** Small objects cost more in the IA classes; combine them into larger objects before a lifecycle transition.

**Review.** [A lifecycle rule moves objects one way to colder classes and then expires them](2-deep.md#a-lifecycle-rule-moves-objects-one-way-to-colder-classes-and-then-expires-them-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q014 -->
### Question 16

A company must keep recordings of customer calls for 10 years to meet a legal rule. The recordings are audio files of 20 MB to 200 MB each, and nobody reads them during normal operations. About twice a year, auditors ask for a few recordings. A wait of up to 48 hours for those recordings is acceptable. The company wants to archive the recordings in Amazon S3. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, and read each requested recording directly with a GET request when the auditors ask.
- Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and restore each requested recording with the Expedited retrieval option when the auditors ask.
- Store the recordings in S3 Standard-IA, and read each requested recording directly with a GET request when the auditors ask.
- Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and restore each requested recording with the Bulk retrieval option when the auditors ask.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and restore each requested recording with the Bulk retrieval option when the auditors ask.

**Deciding phrases.** "nobody reads them during normal operations", "A wait of up to 48 hours", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The recordings are not read in normal operations, so the storage price decides. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours) for long-lived archives. An auditor request starts a restore, and the restored copy is [available only for the duration that you specify](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-temporary-copy). Bulk is the cheapest restore, and its wait fits the 48 hours in the stem.

**Why not.**

- "Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, ...": It works with millisecond reads, but Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours), and the stem accepts a 48-hour wait.
- "Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, ...": From S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the Expedited retrieval option is [Not available](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-deep), so this restore request fails.
- "Store the recordings in S3 Standard-IA, and read ...": It works, but the S3 Glacier classes are [most effective for rarely accessed data](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-classes-min-duration-and-retrieval-fees), and these recordings are read about twice a year.

**Twin.** If the stem said "auditors need a recording within 12 hours" instead: S3 Glacier Deep Archive with a Standard restore, because it finishes [within 12 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-retrieval-standard-default-12-hours-deep-archive).

**Takeaway.** Rarely read archive and a wait of days accepted: S3 Glacier Deep Archive with Bulk restores.

**Review.** [Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects must be restored before anyone reads them](2-deep.md#flexible-retrieval-and-deep-archive-objects-must-be-restored-before-anyone-reads-them-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q016 -->
### Question 17

A hospital group stores medical images in Amazon S3. Each image is between 5 MB and 50 MB, and the images must be kept for many years. Doctors open a given image about once a quarter. When a doctor opens an image, the image must load in real time, within milliseconds. The hospital group wants to reduce its storage costs. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, with an Expedited retrieval request sent each time a doctor opens one of the images.
- S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, with each image read directly by a normal GET request each time a doctor opens it.
- S3 Standard-IA, with each image read directly by a normal GET request each time a doctor opens one of the images.
- S3 Intelligent-Tiering with the Deep Archive Access tier turned on, with each image read by a normal GET request.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, with each image read directly by a normal GET request each time a doctor opens it.

**Deciding phrases.** "about once a quarter", "load in real time, within milliseconds", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval suits data accessed about [once a quarter](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-instant-retrieval-once-a-quarter) that still needs millisecond reads. Its objects are [immediately available using GET](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), with no restore step. Each image is larger than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-glacier-ir-min-size-and-duration), so the minimum billable size does not change the cost.

**Why not.**

- "S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, with an Expedited retrieval ...": Flexible Retrieval data is [archived, and not available for real-time access](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-classes-access-model), and an Expedited restore takes [1–5 minutes](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-flexible).
- "S3 Standard-IA, with each image read directly by ...": It works with the [same latency and throughput performance](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-glacier-ir-vs-standard-ia), but Glacier Instant Retrieval stores images that are read once a quarter for less.
- "S3 Intelligent-Tiering with the Deep Archive Access tier ...": Objects in the Deep Archive Access tier need you to [first restore the object by using RestoreObject](../facts/s3.md#s3-intelligent-tiering-archive-tiers-need-restore), so a GET cannot load them in milliseconds.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Doctors open a given image about once a month" instead: S3 Standard-IA, because Glacier Instant Retrieval has [lower storage costs but higher data access costs](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-glacier-ir-vs-standard-ia).

**Takeaway.** Read about once a quarter, but in milliseconds: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.

**Review.** [Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects must be restored before anyone reads them](2-deep.md#flexible-retrieval-and-deep-archive-objects-must-be-restored-before-anyone-reads-them-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=s3-q018 -->
### Question 18

A company stores build artifacts in an Amazon S3 bucket that has S3 Versioning turned on. The number of current objects stays about the same each month, but the storage bill grows every month. Most of the stored bytes belong to noncurrent object versions. S3 Storage Lens also shows that the bucket has no lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads. The company needs every current version and wants to keep old versions for 30 days. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

- Add a lifecycle rule with the NoncurrentVersionExpiration action that permanently deletes object versions 30 days after they become noncurrent.
- Add a lifecycle rule with an Expiration action for current object versions, so that S3 also removes the parts of incomplete multipart uploads.
- Suspend S3 Versioning on the bucket, so that S3 removes the noncurrent object versions that the bucket already stores.
- Add a lifecycle rule that moves noncurrent object versions to S3 Glacier Deep Archive 30 days after they become noncurrent.
- Add a lifecycle rule with the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action that stops uploads that are not complete 7 days after they start.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Add a lifecycle rule with the NoncurrentVersionExpiration action that permanently deletes object versions 30 days after they become noncurrent.
- Add a lifecycle rule with the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action that stops uploads that are not complete 7 days after they start.

**Deciding phrases.** "noncurrent object versions", "no lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads", "keep old versions for 30 days", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Two things grow. Normal S3 rates [apply for every version of an object](../facts/s3.md#s3-versioning-every-version-billed), so old versions cost money until a rule deletes them. The parts of unfinished uploads also stay stored until the abort action removes them, and [no objects are deleted by this lifecycle action](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-abort-incomplete-multipart).

- This action can [permanently delete noncurrent versions of objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-noncurrent-version-expiration), and the current versions stay untouched.
- This action [stops the multipart upload and deletes the parts](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-abort-incomplete-multipart), so the bytes of unfinished uploads stop growing.

**Why not.**

- "Add a lifecycle rule with an Expiration action ...": Expiration actions [don't remove incomplete multipart uploads](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-expiration-keeps-incomplete-mpu), and expiring current versions hides objects that the company needs.
- "Suspend S3 Versioning on the bucket, so that ...": When versioning is suspended, [existing objects in your bucket do not change](../facts/s3.md#s3-versioning-suspend-keeps-existing-versions), so the old versions keep their storage cost.
- "Add a lifecycle rule that moves noncurrent object ...": It works, but each archived version is billed for at least [180 days](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-min-duration), and the company does not need versions after 30 days.

**Twin.** If the stem said "must keep old versions for 7 years for audits" instead: move noncurrent versions to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours).

**Takeaway.** A versioned bucket that keeps growing: expire noncurrent versions and abort incomplete multipart uploads.

**Review.** [A lifecycle rule moves objects one way to colder classes and then expires them](2-deep.md#a-lifecycle-rule-moves-objects-one-way-to-colder-classes-and-then-expires-them-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
